demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
He is 39, a South Asian man who has built a career as an interior designer, someone who spends his days thinking about space, light, proportion, and how a room can hold a life. When he first speaks about his younger brother's death, he does so in the same careful, controlled way he describes a floor plan: measured, orderly, as if precision might keep something unbearable from spilling out.

Two years ago, his brother dies suddenly in a road accident on the way home from work. There is no warning, no chance to prepare, no bedside conversation, no gradual decline that allows the family to begin grieving before the loss arrives. One phone call changes the shape of his world. He still remembers the exact moment: he is at a client's apartment reviewing fabric samples, his phone vibrating repeatedly in his pocket. At first he ignores it, annoyed by the interruption. Then he sees his cousin's name and answers. He recalls hearing noise in the background, someone crying, and then the words becoming clear only in fragments-accident, hospital, come quickly. By the time he arrives, his brother is already gone.

In the first days afterward, he moves as if on assignment. He helps coordinate family rituals, receives visitors, arranges chairs in the living room for mourners, makes sure water and tea are set out. He notices absurd details-the crooked placement of shoes near the door, the harshness of the overhead lighting, the stain on the rug-and later feels ashamed that his mind lands on these things while his mother is keening in the next room. He tells himself to stay useful. Being useful feels safer than feeling anything at all.

After the funeral, people begin returning to their routines, but he cannot find his own way back. He starts avoiding the road where the accident happened, even when it adds nearly half an hour to his commute. If a client asks him to visit a site near that area, he invents scheduling conflicts and sends a junior colleague instead. He cannot tolerate unexpected phone calls anymore, especially in the evening. When his wife's name flashes on the screen, his chest tightens before he answers. If she is ten minutes late coming home, he imagines twisted metal, a crowd gathering, another call he will have to take.

At work, he remains competent enough that others still describe him as successful. He meets deadlines, produces elegant designs, and can speak convincingly in meetings. Yet the pleasure he once took in his work has thinned out. He used to enjoy visiting showrooms and imagining how a family might live in a space; now he finds himself distracted by danger. He scans for exposed edges, slippery floors, unstable fixtures. During one hotel project, he becomes fixated on whether emergency exits are clearly marked. He tells himself it is professionalism, but he knows it is something else. His mind repeatedly turns ordinary environments into scenes of possible catastrophe.

Sleep becomes unreliable. Some nights he lies awake replaying the call, the hospital corridor, the sight of his brother's still face. Other nights he falls asleep only to wake abruptly, heart pounding, after dreams in which his brother is alive and trying to say something he cannot quite hear. In the morning he feels both shaken and embarrassed. He avoids looking at family photos on his phone, yet he cannot bring himself to delete his brother's number. Every few weeks he opens their old message thread and scrolls upward, reading trivial exchanges about dinner plans or cricket scores, as if enough rereading might produce one more reply.

His wife experiences him as present but far away. He is more irritable than he used to be, snapping over small things-the television volume, dishes left in the sink, a delayed text message. He knows she is trying to be gentle with him, and this sometimes makes him angrier, because it confirms that he has changed. Family gatherings, once noisy and comforting, now feel exhausting. When relatives begin reminiscing about his brother, he often steps outside or volunteers to run an errand. He says he needs air. What he means is that he cannot bear the sudden force of missing him.

He also carries guilt that does not yield to logic. He thinks about the times he ignored his brother's calls because he was busy, the minor argument they had the week before the accident, the fact that he cannot remember the last thing he said to him with certainty. Part of him knows these thoughts are futile, but they return insistently. He wonders whether he has failed his brother by continuing with normal life-choosing paint finishes, discussing budgets, smiling at clients.

Now, when he talks about the future, he does so cautiously. He still loves his family, still goes to work, still performs the roles expected of him. But his life feels partitioned into before and after. He moves through beautifully designed spaces each day while feeling, internally, as though something essential has collapsed. Even in quiet moments at home, seated beside his wife on the sofa they chose together, he waits for the next terrible interruption, unable to trust that ordinary life will remain ordinary.
